newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan caretakers cast doubt on $12bln new city.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan caretakers cast doubt on $12bln new city.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government on Thursday cast doubts over a planned $12 billion high-technology town near Islamabad, calling it a dubious scheme.
Developers had earlier said the Islamabad New City would provide a 21st-century contrast to the rampant decay evident in most Pakistani cities.
But Information Minister Irshad Ahmed Haqqani told a news conference after a meeting of the caretaker cabinet of Prime Minister Meraj Khalid: "The whole scheme is dubious".
He said the government had stopped state television from showing advertisements of the project pending inquiries into the affair.

No comment was immediately available from the officials of the project, a joint venture between the state National Housing Authority and Capital Development Authority and a consortium of 25 local and foreign firms led by a Singapore-based company.
Haqqani declined to specify any suspected wrongdoing when asked if the project, conceived during the period of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, was illegal.
"Unless all the details, all the realities are unearthed, we are not in a position to give an exact answer to this. But I have told you that there are serious doubts in its being genuine," he said.
Project officials had said the city would be equipped with elevated railways, fibre-optic communication systems, security surveillance and garbage recycling.
Private sector participants were to finance the entire project, with no government funds involved.

The government would inquire how the two state organisations lent their names to the project, "whose whole structure is dubious", Haqqani said. "Whoever is found responsible for ignoring his duties as a high official...will be taken to task."
Islamabad New City is planned to spread over 8,260 acres (3,300 hectares) about 12 km (seven miles) south of the Pakistani capital, itself an artificial city built in the 1960s.
It is planned to have its own security agency to deter crime, with closed-circuit cameras monitoring roads, and with residents having a 24-hour hot-line to emergency services.
The project was conceived after Bhutto's government appealed in 1993 for private sector participation in housing ventures.

President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule and appointed Khalid's caretaker government to supervise fresh elections set for February 3 next year.
Bhutto, who denies the charges, filed a petition before the Supreme Court on Wednesday seeking annulment of the presidential order and her reinstatement.
